newsitem.title: FRANCE: Loyal Juppe bows out to shield Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Loyal Juppe bows out to shield Chirac.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe loyally fell on his sword on Monday, accepting blame for two years of austerity and record high unemployment which led to voters humiliating President Jacques Chirac at the ballot box.

In a terse announcement less than 24 hours after his centre-right coalition had trailed the leftist opposition in the first round of parliamentary elections, Juppe said he would quit the premiership no matter who won next Sunday's runoff vote.
"We need a new team led by a new prime minister," he said.
He had earlier hinted he was ready to step aside to give Chirac room for manoeuvre in the event "the sole obstacle to the modernisation and renovation of France is a choice of personality".

French financial markets tumbled and the franc slipped after the first-round vote, in which an alliance of Socialists, Communists and smaller leftist parties outscored the centre-right and appeared poised to take power. This faced the conservative Chirac with the bitter prospect of having to "cohabit" with a hostile government.
The ruling coalition's poor showing put tremendous pressure on its leaders to take dramatic action to turn around the government campaign and give it new life.
To Juppe's dismay, the two-stage vote turned to a large extent into a referendum on his personal record and future.

Juppe, 51, had urged Chirac to call the assembly elections 10 months ahead of time in hopes of winning his government a mandate for bold action during the final five years of Chirac's seven-year presidential term.
During the campaign, polls consistently found fewer than 10 percent of voters in favour of his reappointment.
He soon became the favourite whipping boy both of anxious allies and of political opponents.
Leftists, warning against "five more years of Juppe", had painted him as the embodiment of the austerity and tax rises imposed to help France qualify for a single European currency.
Fellow rightists, sniping at his prickly campaign leadership and his electoral programme, had urged Chirac to jettison him as excess baggage after the election.
Speculation on possible successors has centred on Gaullist ex-premier Edouard Balladur and outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin should the centre-right manage to hold on to power.

Juppe, who currently heads Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party as well as the government, was viewed as a man of great promise when he was elevated to the premiership in May 1995 after two years as a much-admired foreign minster.

Two years later, he has become the focus of voters' anger over record unemployment, public spending cuts, wage freezes for state workers, persistent labour unrest, welfare cut-backs and general grumbling over unkept Chirac campaign promises.
The slim, balding prime minister also suffered from his image as a cold, hard-driving and uncaring technocrat.

To counter his image woes, he had himself photographed in glossy magazines with his wife and infant daughter and penned a short but emotional book, "Entre Nous" (Between Ourselves), in which he admitted to feeling wounded by constant criticism.
He said he had been driven to write it after a woman in Bordeaux, where he is mayor, shouted "Death to idiots" at him in the street.
During the campaign, he tried to take on critics more directly, often with a poignant touch of self-mockery.
Asked in a recent radio interview if he felt stung by the unrelenting personal attacks, he replied: "Everyone says I'm an insensitive computer, so I don't know why you're asking."

Born in the southwestern town of Mont-de-Marsan of modest origins, Juppe attended the elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration (ENA) civil service college before going to work for then-prime minister Chirac as a speechwriter in 1976.
